documents.title: AAGL Practice Report on the Management of Hysteroscopic Distending Media

chunks.content: HIGHLIGHTS Phenylephrine-induced MAP elevation reduces pulmonary edema incidence by 66% in hysteroscopic myomectomy. LUS B-line scores and distention fluid deficit are significantly lower in the phenylephrine group. Phenylephrine lowers TFC at procedure end and decreases furosemide use. During the preparation of this manuscript, the authors utilized Kimi 1.5 to enhance the readability and language clarity. This tool was employed specifically to refine the text and ensure clarity during the revision stage. The authors reviewed and edited the AI-generated content to maintain accuracy and alignment with the study’s objectives. The use of Kimi 1.5 adhered to the TITAN Guideline 2025 [ ] , ensuring transparency and ethical compliance. The authors take full responsibility for the final content and confirm that the AI tool was used in a manner consistent with the guidelines’ recommendations for declaration, purpose, configuration, data safeguards, oversight, and reproducibility. Background Hysteroscopic myomectomy is widely recognized as the first-line conservative surgical treatment for submucosal leiomyomas in women who wish to preserve fertility [ ] . Recent advancements in hysteroscopy techniques have enabled resection of type 3 fibroids [ ] . However, these advances have introduced new challenges, including longer operative times and increased use of distention fluid. Consequently, fluid overload and hysteroscopic intravascular absorption syndrome have become major concerns, threatening patient safety and limiting surgical applications. Although the incidence of hyponatremia has decreased with the discontinuation of hypotonic media, pulmonary edema remains a common complication in patients with fluid overload using isotonic saline [ , ] . There is an urgent need for effective strategies to reduce the incidence of pulmonary edema caused by fluid overload and distention fluid absorption. Fluid overload occurs through the absorption of distention fluid used during operative hysteroscopy, which can disrupt the integrity of venous sinuses and lead to intraperitoneal absorption [ , ] . The pressure gradient between intrauterine pressure (IUP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP) critically affects distention fluid absorption. When IUP exceeds MAP, substantial fluid absorption into the circulation can occur, leading to complications such as pulmonary edema [ , ] . Previous studies have shown that controlling IUP is an effective method to reduce fluid absorption [ , ] . These findings suggest that increasing intraoperative MAP using vasoactive agents such as phenylephrine could reduce the IUP–MAP gradient, thereby decreasing distention fluid absorption and pulmonary edema incidence. However, no studies to date have confirmed this hypothesis. The primary aim of this study was to investigate the effect of increasing the MAP of patients with phenylephrine on pulmonary edema and distention fluid deficit for patients undergoing hysteroscopic myomectomy. We hypothesized that phenylephrine would increase MAP and therefore reduce the incidence of pulmonary edema and distention fluid deficit. Materials and methods This randomized controlled trial was conducted at Tertiary A Hospital between May and December 2024. The study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the institution, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The trial was registered prior to patient enrollment. This manuscript was reported in line with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) Guidelines [ ] . Participants Patients aged 18–60 years with ASA physical status I–II scheduled for elective hysteroscopic myomectomy (Type 2 or 3 per FIGO classification) under general anesthesia and an expected operation time >30 minutes were eligible. Exclusion criteria included BMI >35 kg/m 2 , height <150 cm, weight <45 kg, pregnancy or lactation, abnormal anesthesia history, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular diseases (e.g., hypertension, coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular malformations), cardiopulmonary insufficiency, or refusal to participate. Written informed consent was obtained after routine pre-anesthetic evaluation. Allocation and blinding Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to either the phenylephrine group (Group P) or the control group (Group C). Randomization was performed using PASS 11.0 software with a completely random design. Opaque sealed envelopes containing group assignments were prepared and opened by an anesthesiologist immediately before surgery. The anesthesiologist administered general anesthesia and the study drug infusion but was not involved in data collection or outcome assessment to maintain allocation concealment. The study medication was prepared in identical syringes labeled with the study code, containing either 50 ml of 100 mcg/ml phenylephrine or normal saline. Patients, surgeons, nurses, anesthesia providers, and outcome assessors were blinded to group assignments to minimize bias. Anesthesia protocol Upon arrival in the operating room, standard monitoring was initiated, including SpO 2 , electrocardiography, and blood pressure (BP) measurement via noninvasive oscillometric BP monitoring at 5-minute intervals. Baseline BP was defined as the average of three consecutive MAP measurements with <10% variability. Thoracic electrical bioimpedance (TEB) was measured using the Starling fluid management system (Cheetah Medical Inc., Vancouver, Washington, USA). General anesthesia was induced with intravenous sufentanil (20–25 μg) and propofol (2–2.5 mg/kg). Muscle relaxation was achieved with succinylcholine (1–1.5 mg/kg), followed by endotracheal intubation. After intubation, end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO₂) monitoring was initiated.

Anesthesia protocol Upon arrival in the operating room, standard monitoring was initiated, including SpO 2 , electrocardiography, and blood pressure (BP) measurement via noninvasive oscillometric BP monitoring at 5-minute intervals. Baseline BP was defined as the average of three consecutive MAP measurements with <10% variability. Thoracic electrical bioimpedance (TEB) was measured using the Starling fluid management system (Cheetah Medical Inc., Vancouver, Washington, USA). General anesthesia was induced with intravenous sufentanil (20–25 μg) and propofol (2–2.5 mg/kg). Muscle relaxation was achieved with succinylcholine (1–1.5 mg/kg), followed by endotracheal intubation. After intubation, end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO₂) monitoring was initiated. Mechanical ventilation was set to volume-controlled mode with a tidal volume of 6–8 ml/kg, respiratory rate of 10–12 breaths/min, and PEEP of 5 cm H₂O. Anesthesia was maintained with continuous infusion of propofol (6–8 mg/kg/h) and remifentanil (0.05–0.25 μg/kg/min). Cisatracurium (5 mg) was administered intraoperatively to maintain muscle relaxation. At the end of surgery, all anesthetics were discontinued, and neuromuscular blockade was reversed with neostigmine (0.5 mg) and glycopyrrolate (0.25 mg). Patients were then transferred to the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU). In the PACU, patients were managed by anesthesiologists and nurses who were blinded to group assignments. Routine postoperative assessments included checking for bulbar conjunctival edema. If edema was detected, furosemide (20 mg) was administered. If mask oxygen failed to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 90%, patients received either noninvasive positive pressure ventilation or intubation and mechanical ventilation at the anesthesiologist’s discretion. Patients were transferred to the ward once their Steward Score exceeded 4. Intervention After intubation, all patients received the study drug infusion initiated at 10 ml/h. In Group C, the infusion rate remained constant during surgery. In contrast, in Group P, the anesthesiologist adjusted the infusion to maintain MAP at 100–120% of baseline. The target MAP in Group P was set at 120% of baseline. If MAP did not reach the target, the infusion rate was increased. Conversely, if BP exceeded 120% of baseline, the infusion was reduced or stopped. If BP remained above 120% of baseline, the anesthesiologist increased the remifentanil infusion rate. If BP remained elevated despite remifentanil, nicardipine (0.2 mg) was administered. Distention fluid management Normal saline was used as the distention medium. Due to the limitations of the equipment available at our institution, we do not have an automated fluid management system as recommended by the AAGL guidelines [ ] . Instead, we used a distention meter that only sets the output pressure (Fig. ). As no device was available to directly measure IUP, the output pressure setting of the distention device was adjusted based on the surgeon’s intraoperative assessment to ensure optimal visualization. The initial output pressure setting was at 22 kPa. If hysteroscopic visualization was limited, the surgeon increased the distention pressure to improve clarity. It is important to note that the actual IUP during surgery is typically lower than the set distention output pressure due to the leakage at the junction of instrument components and resistance at the inflow and outflow ports [ ] . To avoid gas embolism, the distention fluid in our institution was connected to the hysteroscopic inflow port through an infusion device (Fig. ). Murphy’s droppers incorporated in the infusion set facilitate the observation of air entry and ensure the continuity of fluid flow, thereby preventing air from entering the uterine cavity. However, these droppers also contribute to the transmission loss of distention pressure, further reducing the actual IUP. In two pilot cases, we measured IUP using the TruWave PX260 transducer (Edwards Lifesciences Corporation), a device originally designed for BP measurement. The recorded IUP during surgery stabilized between 90 and 95 mmHg, with peaks remaining below 100 mmHg – within the recommended safe threshold [ ] . A dedicated nurse managed the distention fluid, which was collected in a specialized bag. Any spilled fluid was absorbed by pre-weighed dry drapes, and its volume was calculated. Distention fluid deficit was calculated by subtracting total outflow (collected bag volume plus spilled fluid) from total inflow, with final measurements recorded at procedure completion. According to ISGE guidelines [ ] , procedures were closely monitored by anesthesiology if the fluid deficit exceeded 1000 ml, with consideration given to termination. Deficits of over 2500 ml need immediate termination of surgery. The final decision to continue or terminate surgery was made collaboratively by the anesthesiologist and surgeon, based on a comprehensive risk-benefit assessment of continuing versus staging the procedure. Outcome measures The primary outcome was pulmonary edema incidence diagnosed by lung ultrasound (LUS) [ ] . LUS was performed by a blinded investigator immediately before extubation. Patients were placed supine, and a 3.5 MHz convex probe was used. The anterior and lateral chest walls were divided into eight zones (four per side), with the clavicle to the third intercostal space designated as the upper region and the third intercostal space to the diaphragm as the lower region. Each zone was systematically scanned. B-lines were defined as hyperechoic lines perpendicular to the pleural line [ ] . Presence of three or more B-lines across the eight zones was considered positive. Pulmonary edema was diagnosed if at least two positive areas were present [ ] . The total B-line score was the sum of B-lines across all eight regions. Secondary outcomes included B-line scores, thoracic fluid content (TFC) at the end of operation, ∆TFC (∆TFC = TFC at the end of operation − baseline TFC), distention fluid deficit, furosemide use, surgical visual field score (assessed using a visual ambiguity score from 0 to 10 by the surgeon), intraoperative blood loss (estimated and recorded by the surgeon), and adverse effects. Additionally, patient demographic data, myoma characteristics (depth, diameter, classification), multiple myomas, use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), operation duration, output pressure setting of the distention device, intraoperative fluid infusion volume, and intraoperative mean MAP were documented. Mean intraoperative MAP was calculated as the average of all recorded MAP measurements. Statistical methods Based on our pilot study ( n = 10), pulmonary edema incidence after hysteroscopic myomectomy was 80%, and we estimated that phenylephrine infusion could reduce it by 50%. The estimated sample size was 20 patients per group, with a power of 80% and a type I error of 0.05. The sample size was increased to 44 to account for potential dropouts. Statistics were performed using IBM SPSS 29.0 and GraphPad Prism 9.0. The normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Continuous variables are presented as the means ± SDs or medians with IQRs, depending on whether they were normally distributed. Student’s t -test was used for analysis of normally distributed variables, and Mann–Whitney U -test was used for analysis of nonnormally distributed variables. Categorical variables are presented as numbers (%). The Pearson χ 2 test or the Fisher’s exact test was performed to compare categorical variables. 95% CIs were estimated using the Hodges–Lehmann estimate. Further, in order to explore the relationships between B-line scores, distention fluid deficits, TFC at the end of operation, and ∆TFC, Spearman correlation analysis was performed. Additionally, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to independently evaluate each potential predictor of pulmonary edema and calculate the Youden index. The maximum Youden index cutoff point was used as its diagnostic cutoff value, and the sensitivity and specificity were calculated. P -values were two-sided, with a P -value less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. Theory The theoretical basis of our study is that distention fluid absorption during hysteroscopic procedures is driven by the pressure gradient between IUP and MAP. When IUP exceeds MAP, distention fluid is driven into the systemic circulation, potentially causing fluid overload and pulmonary edema. We hypothesized that increasing MAP with phenylephrine infusion reduces this gradient, thereby decreasing fluid absorption. Phenylephrine, a selective α1-adrenergic agonist, increases systemic vascular resistance and MAP via vasoconstriction. By elevating MAP, we aimed to counteract elevated IUP, reducing the pressure gradient and fluid absorption into the circulation. This approach offers a novel strategy for fluid management during hysteroscopic procedures. Results Of the 46 patients assessed for eligibility, 44 were enrolled and randomly assigned to either Group P or Group C, with 22 patients in each group. No surgeries required termination. Fluid deficits exceeding 2500 ml were found in eight patients postoperatively. All randomized patients finished the operation were included in the final analysis (Fig. ). Baseline demographic and surgical characteristics were comparable between groups (Table ). Baseline MAP did not differ between groups; however, intraoperative mean MAP was significantly higher in Group P than in Group C [mean difference = 17.4 mmHg, 95% CI (11.2–23.5), P < 0.01]. Postoperative pulmonary edema was diagnosed in 16 patients by LUS. Pulmonary edema incidence was significantly lower in Group P (18.2%) than in Group C (54.6%) [RR = 0.33, 95% CI (0.13–0.81), P = 0.027, Table ]. Furthermore, Group P exhibited significantly lower LUS B-line scores at the end of the operation compared to Group C ( P = 0.016, Fig. A). Pulmonary edema incidence was significantly lower in Group P (18.2%) than in Group C (54.6%) [RR = 0.33, 95% CI (0.13–0.81), P = 0.027, Table ]. Furthermore, Group P exhibited significantly lower LUS B-line scores at the end of the operation compared to Group C ( P = 0.016, Fig. A). The incidence of distention fluid deficit ≥2500 ml was lower in Group P than in Group C, but the difference was not statistically significant ( P = 0.24). Distention fluid deficits in Group P were significantly lower than that in Group C ( P = 0.018, Fig. B). Fourteen patients received furosemide. Among them, three patients in Group C developed bilateral rales and required additional furosemide, while none in Group P showed similar symptoms. Furosemide was also significantly lower than that in Group C ( P = 0.022). No patients developed hypoxemia or required noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation. TFC at the end of operation and ∆TFC were significantly lower than that in Group C ( P < 0.01, see Fig. C and D). Surgical visual field score did not significantly differ between groups [9 (2) in Group P vs. 9 (1.25) in Group C, MD = 0, 95% CI (−1 to 0), P = 0.39]. Estimated blood loss was also similar between groups [125 (150) in Group P vs. 200 (200) in Group C, MD = 50, 95% CI (−100 to 0), P = 0.089]. B-line scores correlated significantly with distention fluid deficits, TFC at the end of operation, and ∆TFC ( P ≤ 0.001, see Table ). The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for distention fluid deficit, TFC at the end of operation and ∆TFC in diagnosing pulmonary edema were 0.85, 0.73, and 0.83, respectively (see Fig. ). The best cutoff values were 1900 ml, 49.0/kΩ, and 7.1/kΩ, respectively. Discussion This is the first prospective randomized controlled trial investigating the effects of phenylephrine-induced MAP elevation on pulmonary edema and distention fluid deficit in hysteroscopic myomectomy patients. Phenylephrine administration significantly increased MAP, reduced postoperative pulmonary edema incidence, lowered LUS B-line scores, decreased distention fluid deficit, and minimized diuretic use. Additionally, both TFC at the end of surgery and ∆TFC were significantly lower in the phenylephrine group than in controls. These findings propose a novel intraoperative fluid management strategy that improves patient outcomes and expands the feasibility of hysteroscopic myomectomy. The integration of TFC and LUS enables early detection of subclinical pulmonary edema, emphasizing the need for vigilant monitoring, while defined risk stratification thresholds allow for timely intervention. Moreover, phenylephrine-based fluid management may broaden eligibility for hysteroscopic myomectomy, permitting complete myoma resection in a single procedure for patients who would otherwise require multiple surgeries due to fluid overload. This approach enhances clinical success while reducing the surgical burden on patients. These results are mainly attributable to reduced driving pressure for fluid absorption achieved by increasing MAP. Elevating MAP without altering IUP decreases the pressure gradient driving fluid absorption. MAP approximates uterine extravascular tissue resistance, and the IUP–MAP gradient determines distention fluid absorption [ ] , with greater pressure gradients driving increased fluid uptake. Previous studies have shown that controlling IUP effectively reduces fluid deficit [ , , ] . Our study innovatively found that increasing MAP with phenylephrine also effectively reduced the distention fluid deficit ( P < 0.05). Considering perioperative BP management guidelines recommending BP within ±20% of baseline [ ] , we set the intraoperative MAP target at 120% of baseline. However, without continuous invasive monitoring, mean MAP in the phenylephrine group only reached baseline levels (Baseline MAP 90.7 ± 8.9 vs. Intraoperative mean MAP 90.8 ± 11.4). Despite this, maintaining MAP at baseline was sufficient to significantly reduce distention fluid deficit and pulmonary edema incidence ( P < 0.05). Further research is needed to determine the optimal MAP increase to maximally reduce fluid deficit. Phenylephrine, a selective α1-adrenergic agonist, is widely used clinically to increase BP via vasoconstriction. In this study, phenylephrine was used to elevate intraoperative MAP. Given the established presence of adrenergic receptors in the uterus [ ] , it is plausible that phenylephrine activated adrenergic α1-receptors in the uterus, thereby promoting uterine contraction and reducing the deficit of uterine distention fluid. This potential mechanism requires further investigation. The effects of other vasoactive agents on distention fluid deficit should also be explored in future studies. This potential mechanism requires further investigation. The effects of other vasoactive agents on distention fluid deficit should also be explored in future studies. Another strength of this study is the use of LUS to assess and quantify pulmonary edema during hysteroscopic surgery. Compared with hypotonic and electrolyte-free media, fluid overload with isotonic media such as saline is less likely to cause hypo-osmolality or hyponatremia. However, hypervolemia and subsequent pulmonary edema or congestive heart failure remain concerns. LUS is a highly sensitive diagnostic tool for detecting extravascular lung water. LUS has been reported to be more sensitive than chest X-ray for detecting pulmonary edema in patients with acute decompensated heart failure, with 88% sensitivity and 90% specificity [ ] . Therefore, we used LUS at the end of surgery to diagnose pulmonary edema and quantify its severity using B-line scores. Correlation analysis also revealed a significant correlation between B-line scores and distention fluid deficit ( P < 0.05). To our knowledge, no study reported the incidence of pulmonary edema during hysterescopy. Most studies reported the incidence of fluid overload using absolute distention fluid deficit as the standard. Notably, LUS use enabled early detection of subclinical pulmonary edema. Some patients diagnosed with pulmonary edema had no obvious clinical symptoms and did not require furosemide treatment, which may not have been recorded in previous studies. However, these patients still require close postoperative monitoring. Early detection of subclinical pulmonary edema is essential to prevent complications and ensure patient safety. Nevertheless, in our study, pulmonary edema incidence detected by LUS and B-line scores, as well as furosemide use, were significantly lower in Group P than in Group C. Beyond LUS, we also compared TFC between groups. TFC, measured by TEB, is calculated as the inverse of thoracic impedance [ , ] and correlates positively with thoracic fluid volume, serving as a predictor of pulmonary edema presence and severity [ ] . In our study, TFC at the end of surgery and ∆TFC also showed significant correlations with B-line scores. TFC at the end of operation and ∆TFC were significantly lower in the Group P, further supporting the intervention’s effectiveness. To further explore the diagnostic utility of these parameters, we conducted ROC curve analyses. ROC analysis showed that AUCs for distention fluid deficit, end-surgery TFC, and ΔTFC in diagnosing pulmonary edema were 0.85, 0.73, and 0.83, respectively. These results suggest that, compared with TFC at the end of operation, distention fluid deficit and ΔTFC are more accurate in diagnosing pulmonary edema and can effectively identify at-risk patients, aiding early intervention and management. Limitation This study has several limitations to consider when interpreting its results. First, this study used a single-blind rather than a double-blind design. Blinding the attending anesthesiologist was not feasible or safe due to the intervention’s nature and need for real-time monitoring and anesthesia adjustment. However, to minimize bias, other study personnel, including outcome assessors, were blinded to treatment allocation. Second, the study population consisted mainly of young, healthy patients with ASA I–II status. This limits generalizability to patients with severe comorbidities or higher surgical risk. Third, due to the limited sample size, multivariate logistic regression could not be performed to evaluate factors associated with postoperative pulmonary edema. Instead, Spearman correlation analyses were used to explore variable relationships. This approach does not control for confounders, limiting definitive causal conclusions. Future studies with larger samples are needed. Fourth, normal saline was used as the distention fluid. Effects of other hypotonic or electrolyte-free distention fluids, such as glycine, were not evaluated and may differ regarding fluid deficit and hemodynamic impact. Further research is needed to confirm applicability to other distention fluids used in hysteroscopic surgery. Finally, direct IUP measurement was not performed due to the lack of specialized equipment. Nevertheless, standardized protocols ensured consistent distention pressure across all procedures. We also monitored and maintained comparable distention device output pressure settings between groups. While this methodology provided a stable surgical field, we acknowledge that direct IUP quantification would yield greater precision. Future studies should employ dedicated IUP monitoring devices to better elucidate its relationship with MAP and fluid absorption. Conclusion This randomized controlled trial demonstrates that phenylephrine-induced MAP elevation significantly reduces pulmonary edema incidence and distention fluid deficit during hysteroscopic myomectomy. Maintaining MAP at baseline with phenylephrine effectively lowers LUS B-line scores, TFC, and furosemide use. Distention fluid deficit, TFC, and ΔTFC significantly correlated with B-line scores, and ROC analysis identified thresholds for early risk stratification. These findings support phenylephrine as a viable intraoperative fluid management strategy in hysteroscopic surgery, warranting further research on optimal MAP targets and broader applicability across patient populations
